Please watch the following videos so you are prepared to work on these skills in class. For those of you repeating this class, please work on a more complex trick behavior that utilizes each of these skills.

Working with Target Sticks:

We will work on this next week but if you have time to practice this along with hand touch, these two things are usually easy to train in the same short session. All we are looking for at this point is your dog touching the stick with its nose with a little effort to move forward to reach it, marking the correct response & reinforcing the behavior by “paying” with a treat.

You can use anything you want for a target stick. A cheap & easy one to find is a paint stirrer from Lowes or Home Depot, wooden spoon, ruler, etc. At this point, no need to run out & get a fancy target stick, we are just trying to teach our dog to nose touch an object that is an extension of your hand.

title: Tricks - Week #5 (Spring '26) - Prep for Take/Hold/Carry/Give and some New Trick Ideas
body:
We will work to SHAPE mouthwork.  We want to make sure this is fun & pleasant for the dogs. Please collect a few items to bring to class with different textures (wood, plastic, cloth, metal, etc.) for shaping the take/hold if you can gather some. Try to find items your dog won't find objectionable or uncomfortably sized. Please NEVER force a dog to put an object in its mouth. You will create aversion to it. Wait until class if you are at all unsure about how to proceed.

Always take your time with mouthwork training sessions. Please don’t push too hard, fast, or use anything resembling force holds. Use short sessions & stop on a positive note. Just a few attempts & then work on something different or take a break. 

This can be frustrating for the dog & handler if you find objects that the dog doesn’t like to hold or you get stuck and allow frustration. Try to avoid those things & find something fun like a toy that the dog is happy to hold if you’re running into resistance. Making little bits of progress with a happy, motivated dog will go a lot farther than pushing a reluctant dog into doing a trick that it hates.

I am providing these videos so you are familiar with the type of training we will start next week and be ready to start in class. Familiarize yourself with them & I would rather you wait until class to start work than doing anything that impedes progress or creates aversion.

title: Tricks - Week #6 (Spring '26) - Mouth Work & New Trick Ideas
body:
I would like to see everyone working on take/hold/carry/give at whatever level you are with your dog. Please take time to build the strongest foundation for the hold and grip with your dog. Make sure you're not reinforcing an early object spit or you're going to have a solid retrieve that ends with dropping the object prematurely. Plan your sessions to prevent reinforcing bad habits.

Keep in mind the easiest way to create sloppy or incomplete retrieves is to just throw objects & expect formal performance. That should be reserved for play. Teaching a formal retrieve is very different from a backyard game of fetch. Having said that, when your dog is refusing or reluctant to take objects in its mouth, the best way to start is using a chase the object game or pretend you are playing keepaway to get the dog reaching for it with its mouth WHILE YOU HAVE A SOLID HOLD ON THE OBJECT.

Use objects your dog will find pleasant to put in its mouth. The more pleasant or fun you make it, the better results you will have. Metal is notoriously objectionable for many dogs to hold. Add to the variety of textures slowly once you have success with things dogs typically are willing to mouth like leather, wood, plastic, etc.

Last week's email had a variety of information that should fit every dog in the class. My recommendation would be to practice at least one step lower than you feel your dog is successful. Make that stronger before moving on, i.e., if your dog is taking objects in its mouth but is not holding firmly (rolling the object in its mouth, or spitting it out before you have asked), you should go back to very beginning steps until you get a good, solid hold. Keep a hold on the object to prevent rehearsal of bad habits (like rolling or spitting early).

Of all the behaviors that we try to teach in this class, this is the one most people rush & get very sloppy results. The types of tricks you can build from solid mouth work will never end once your dog is fluent.

Show me some successful progression in your dog's mouth work next week & we will work to see how we can advance each individual dog.

New Trick Ideas

Here are some fun new tricks to try. Most of them use luring or targeting foundations that your dogs should be very fluent performing now that we are ending week 6.



Balancing a Treat (Intermediate)

Here is a good method to show Balancing a treat (you may want to use a non-treat item when starting balance if your dog is very excited about the food. I use about a 1" square piece of cardboard when starting this trick.).

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1SnosqL28Mo

I hope this helps!  Make sure to continue foundation work on chin rest. It has millions of uses but will be especially useful getting calm acceptance of food or objects coming toward the dog's nose. 

Circle Backwards around Handler/Orbit (Advanced)

This is a fun & flashy trick. This is a good one for freestyle routines too.

https://youtu.be/hdstpURNaoI

https://youtu.be/ZyGC7eWh8Ys



Slide into the Middle (Advanced)

This trick is another fun movement trick. It can also be very useful in real life situations. For nervous or excitable dogs, there is something about moving into a sit or down between the handler's legs that is very calming (much like the Peekaboo trick that can also be used in this way). It is a great spot to easily distract your dog with food if an unexpected event happens or use it as a calming exercise before heading into a trial ring.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aYmzD77MF0A



Rebound Off Wall or Object (Advanced)

https://www.instagram.com/reels/DR5URbQkuY3/



Rebound Off Handler (Advanced)

Be careful if you're going to try this one! Some dogs might like this one a little too much. With the big dogs, this could be a serious hazard. Use your best judgment on this one & take your own mobility into consideration along with your dog's size, fitness, and impulse control. If you are at all unsteady on your feet or you have a large dog, I suggest you try the Rebound Off Wall or Object.

https://www.facebook.com/reel/6835826799863005

https://www.youtube.com/shorts/byxUegNuSl4

https://www.youtube.com/shorts/e_CavsxaDE4

https://www.facebook.com/reel/2697832823749417

https://www.facebook.com/reel/852905740902551



Hopscotch (Advanced) 


Here's another fun trick that uses foot targeting foundations. 

https://www.youtube.com/shorts/ZwKzqr2icgc

Waiter, No Veggies, please! (Performer)

Here's a fun combination of cues (they are off camera). The dog rings a bell, and refuses the vegetables or gets a meaty treat. Your dog can turn away for the veggies (I suggest you use plastic grocery toy veggies so the trick can travel with you) and regular real meat treats.

You can also combine this trick idea with "yes" or "no" when presenting the meat or veggie.

https://www.facebook.com/1484591725181044/videos/308505573174931


Nod your head "yes" (Performer - Answer Questions) 

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ITU1RTnnXh8

For this trick, I suggest you also consider training it similar to the "no" below. I find it easier using an actual nose target on a high & low surface just like she will use training the "no" below.

Shake your Head "no" (Performer - Answer Questions)

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-XUwoRVuWp8

I hope you'll give some of these a try. Most of these are real crowd pleasers & are fun to teach.

Have a great week!

title: Tricks - Week #7 (Spring '26) - Some New Tricks
body:
Some New Tricks for you to start to work toward. Have fun this week. Keep working those foundations & let's see some progress on your Dog Who Reads!

Shell Game (Intermediate)
(Nose Work dogs can use scents)

More info on the shell game that we discussed in class. This is a real crowd pleaser & an easy one to teach.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=grCNnzxJQgQ


Sit Pretty (including fading lure) (Advanced)

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IQUerO0woqw

She demonstrates a couple of methods with different dogs. I hope one of those will work for you.

Take a Bow (Advanced)

Remember, timing on this trick is really important so I recommend using the clicker until you have the fluent behavior on cue.  After that, a voice marker works great.

There are a variety of ways to train this behavior. I am sharing a few common methods below.

Personally, I also give the dog a front paw target while luring the front end down until the elbows bend making sure timing on the mark is good. That paw target gives the dog a starting point & tells the dog its front feet should stay in position while moving into the bow. I like using a 2x4 board but any kind of foot target would work.

Also, a simple capture works great. I believe I told you the story at the beginning of class about the handler who decided to take her clicker to bed with her to make sure she remembered to have it ready when she let her dog out of the crate in the morning to capture the "bow" which was really just a stretch she put on cue.

I especially like how this trainer rewards the dog by tossing the treat forward to make sure the dog doesn't get into the habit of collapsing into a down position.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6TZUEOV9-nQ

Another method

Part 1

Walking Handstand (Performer)

This behavior takes a lot of time & conditioning core muscles. Not all dogs in the class are ready for this full trick, but several are. All of you can work on the basics to walk backward into position with back end up off the ground if it is a trick you'd like to train.

This is a very advanced behavior, but the basics are things anyone in the class can do with their dog.

A couple of great how-to videos here:

Remember, even if you are at a higher level, Intermediate & Advanced tricks that you didn't use to gain your title are used in Performer & Performer Elite levels.

Have fun this week!

title: Tricks - Week #8 (Spring '26) - More fun Tricks
body:
We have 2 weeks left in classes so I hope you will find some of the tricks I've sent you or that we've worked on in class to add to the titles you've already completed. I will keep uncompleted title sheets after class ends so there's no need to panic, but I always like to complete as many titles as possible during the class session. 

Let me know if you need help between now & class. I suggest going through the checklists to see if there are some tricks to complete your current title between now & the end of class.

Go back through the class emails to find some tricks you never got a chance to try. The more you work with your trick dog, the easier it becomes for them to start offering behaviors & you just might find that a trick that seemed impossible is now very workable.

Here are a few more ideas that you might find fun.

Spatula Treat Flip/Catch

We played with this a little in class this week. I think it will help speed up the process of the dog expecting a treat to fly in the air if you start by tossing the treat when the dog paws the spatula. Half of the trick is the catch & that's a skill that just comes with practice. Beyond that, there aren't a whole lot of ideas to get this trick perfected. So much will depend on the angle of the spatula, the treat you choose, your dog's pawing motion, ability to catch, etc. Give it a shot, it's just too much fun not to try.

title: Tricks - Week #1 (Summer '26) - Welcome to Tricks Class
body:
Welcome to Tricks Class where fun is the #1 goal while you gain some new skills to teach your dog tricks. Each dog will be different and we will find your individual dog’s strengths so you can bring out its inner superstar. In my emails, I will give you videos to demonstrate skills we are working on as reinforcement to classwork and some upcoming ideas. That will help you work at your own pace but also give you some reference after class is over.

Several in this class are returning for the second, third, or more sessions of this class. Most of this week's emails will be duplicates of emails sent last session but upcoming weeks will be more individualized for the current class. The concepts in these intro emails make strong foundations or strengthen them, so I hope you'll review them.  Remember, next week, no dogs are needed in class. If you need to bring your dog to class, please bring a crate. We consider Week #2 to be the most important class of the session (not to mention, probably the most fun.). 

Please don’t think there is a time limit on any specific trick or lesson. Work at the pace that fits you and your dog. Some tricks may not be appropriate for your dog due to limitations, age, etc. That’s fine, don’t force the issue, there will be other tricks for your dog if you skip certain things. Also, if you feel any trick will be counterproductive to other training you are doing, please use your judgment.

There will be no "Week 10 Test". Instead, we will keep active records of your progress working toward the titles offered by AKC. I will keep those forms so they don't get lost. I suggest you keep track of your progress on the sheets that I will be sending in a separate email. It's up to you to decide if you want to actually send them into AKC for your titles and that is not a requirement of this class.

There are lots of methods to teach the same behaviors. Keep this in mind when I send multiple videos that aren’t exactly what we discuss in class. I try to give you variations so you can choose the style you like best. Different dogs respond better to different methods.

Please don’t let any individual trick or type of training intimidate you and know there are plenty of other tricks for your dog if one doesn’t fit your goals. We will work together to tailor this to you and your dog. Some dogs like to use paws, some mouths, some movement, etc. Be looking for those clues during this class and we’ll use that info to train cool tricks that come more naturally to your dog.

Tricks would be boring if all dogs did the same tricks the same way. The structure of some breeds makes certain tricks less desirable or even dangerous. Please try to use good judgment for your dog and remember you aren’t required to perform any specific tricks. Keep your dog’s safety in mind at all times. Long-backed dogs have different limitations that a more moderately-structured 4-year-old dog can safely perform, etc.

Terms to be familiar with regarding the styles of training we will use are below. We will go into lots more detail in upcoming classes so don’t worry if they are unfamiliar to you now. I’m providing this info so you have an idea where we are heading and the skills you’ll use to train tricks.

LURING: Typically uses a food reward to guide the dog into position. We will also use tools like hand targets or target sticks as lures that are precursors to rewards.

CAPTURING: When we ‘catch’ a dog in the act of spontaneously performing a behavior and mark the behavior we would like the dog to repeat. With good timing, effective markers, followed by consistent reinforcement, we can then put those behaviors on cue.

SHAPING: using successive approximations of a behavior by breaking that behavior down into tiny increments. We reinforce the dog at each incremental step toward the desired goal until you've achieved the full behavior.

Shaping: Process of marking and rewarding (Click/Treat = C/T) small increments of behavior toward an end result
Free Shaping: No indication of intended behavior from the handler. The dog is free to offer behaviors. This method requires the most handler skill.
Shaping with Environmental Management: Manipulating the dog’s environment to get the highest number of correct responses in the shortest period of time.
Shaping with Prompts:
Targeting — (target sticks, platforms, targets, props)
Learned behavior that directs the dog.
Shortens learning time

Anywhere you use a clicker, you can use a verbal marker. The important part is that you consider a click or mark to be a “contract” with your dog and that you reinforce every time you mark a behavior (even if your timing was off and it was a bad click/mark).

MARKER TRAINING:  Remember that Clicker training = Marker training. There is no distinction, as long as you are marking the correct response and your timing is suitable. Clickers make it easier to mark the precise moment in time but that is the only reason why I prefer training new behaviors with a clicker. After the behavior is learned, I quickly phase out the clicker on that behavior and use voice markers instead.
NO MODELING:  We will not use any form of Modeling in this class. Modeling is a technique used in traditional training to get the behavior. At the outset, the dog is physically guided, compelled, forced, physically manipulated, intimidated, or punished into performing a behavior. Pulling up on the leash attached to a collar and pushing down on a dog's butt into a sit is an example of modeling. There’s no fun in that so we won’t use this method.

NO CORRECTIONS:  We will not be using corrections because we want the dog to learn it is free to experiment. That will encourage them to think and problem-solve. If we aren’t getting the result we want, we’re going to try a new approach rather than correct or force the dog. Try not to use the word, “NO” (or other interrupting sounds) and use the dog’s successes with positive reinforcement for motivation. Ignore incorrect responses and reinforce the correct ones (or things that are closer to the end behavior). This is a hard one for all of us, but I’d like everybody to make the effort to avoid “NO” when training tricks.

I look forward to seeing you in class. Let me know if you have questions or want more info. I’ll be happy to help. Get ready to have some fun. Please make sure to have an easy-access treat pouch loaded with small treats, easily chewable, high-value preferred. I recommend two kinds of treats (one extra high value to your dog).

I know there is a lot of info in these Week #1 emails. This is just to get us started. Please don’t feel overwhelmed if it seems like a lot of info. There are no deadlines and, I promise, most of my emails won’t be this wordy or such a bombardment. I just want you to have access to the info so that when you are ready to use it, it’s here for you. The most important rule in this class is we are having fun with no pressure or deadlines!!!

title: Tricks - (Summer '26) - Fun Shaping Session & a Surprise
body:
If you've ever wondered what I'm doing before dawn, I'm looking for cool videos to share with the class, of course. Seriously though, this is a great example of an awesome shaping session. It also includes an unexpected event. This is a  great way to show you how to respond when it happens to you. I don't often find online videos that show mid-session "fails" that turn out to be so successful and descriptive.

https://www.facebook.com/reel/131366253403425

First, let me say this dog's handler has obviously done a lot of shaping with this dog. Most dogs aren't this quick & she is able to increase criteria very fast. Evidence of an experienced dog is clear with an experienced handler who uses shaping in much of her training. Don't expect your dogs to progress this quickly on a behavior this sophisticated until you and your dog have far more shaping experience.

I'm sharing this because the communication with the dog is very good. Her timing is good & she is not muddying communication by trying to "help" her dog by luring, talking, coaching, nothing ... just the click.

Take note of how she ignores the behavior when the dog goes off course. That was so cute regardless of what her real criteria was! Why did that happen? She tried to raise criteria a little too fast, the dog decided to offer a completely new behavior to try to get her to click. 

Another thing to take note of here is that her training area is very clear of distractions (in our eyes). The dog, however, was very aware of that wall in the background and used it as an attempt to get another click when the click was withheld for so long, The dog assumed it was wrong so it changed course. It's easy for me to critique that because I have had the benefit of watching the video a dozen times. In the moment, we all make these kinds of "mistakes" and dogs recover quickly when we respond with clear communication. Don't let that discourage you. it is all part of it. 

Have a great day!

Jeanne

title: Week #2 (Summer '26) - New Foundation Skill - Shaping a Behavior
body:
Homework 

Please watch the following video several times. I also recommend you revisit this video in future weeks to sharpen your skills. You will build a strong foundation for targeting & interacting with new objects if you regularly practice variations of this seemingly simple clicker game. This video is an example of a practical application of the skills we learned in class.

https://youtu.be/EP7Soem31qg?si=16wccxkVN2XzGtfP 

The most significant thing I'd like you to think about with this video is that shaping is teaching your dog how to think. When we don't correct our dogs, lure, or physically manipulate our dogs, we allow them to think. When they think through a problem, they retain what they have learned.

Think about the shaping game we played with humans & note how clear her communication is with her dog.  This type of training not only helps you create a thinking dog, dogs retain what they have learned longer, and they will work to get you to engage with them by offering behaviors.

This video is an excellent example of “shaping” a behavior. Melanie & I will often refer to this behavior as "The Mat Game". Not only is Kay Laurence demonstrating shaping, she also is teaching the invaluable skill of ‘going to a mat or stationary object’. The dog is learning self-control by staying on the mat and the ability to stop & wait for another command or cue.

1. She charges the clicker noise by throwing a treat and getting the dog to orient back to her.

2. Notice how her body posture and behavior is completely still & not distracting. She isn’t luring, directing, or using her voice.

3. The dog becomes mentally engaged & starts offering behavior to make her click and treat.  

4.  Once the dog is mentally engaged and offering behaviors, then she introduces the mat. Instead of expecting all 4 feet on the mat, Kay breaks the behavior down into small increments, such as looking at the mat, moving toward the mat, one foot on the mat, two feet on the mat etc. 
 
4. As the dog progresses, she increases the criteria so that the dog learns more of his body should be on the mat. By breaking the behavior down in small increments, she is able to keep the reward level high but also teach the dog that if she doesn’t click, then he should try a different behavior to force the click.  The dog is communicating with her with his behavior!

Note:

The timing of the click tells the dog it is correct. 
If she doesn’t click, the dog corrects itself
Her food placement after the click (behind, left, right, front) resets the dog off the mat so he must reorient to the mat to make the game continue. 
Since Kay isn’t giving the dog hints on what to do, the dog must work through the puzzle by offering behavior. The mental process of working out the puzzle often makes the behavior much stronger for the dog than luring etc.

This video went missing from YouTube for a couple of our class sessions, so I really hope it stays online. This skill is so valuable for tricks where a dog needs to get to a location & perform another behavior, or just stop in a specific position. 

Her technique is precise & her communication with the dog is flawless with nothing more than clicks. I could hold an entire class discussing all the intricate details going on in this simple training session, but the more familiar you become with shaping, the more you will see them without my pointing them out. 

Some additional things to take note of:
She isn't talking, coaching, luring, or directing her dog in any way.
Her clicks are timed properly to signal to the dog exactly when her dog is correct.
Her clicks mark & reward tiny increments toward the end goal.
Look how quickly the dog "corrects itself" simply because she doesn't click & treat.
Her dog is literally thinking. He's thinking about what he needs to do to get that click & reward. When he doesn't get it, he thinks through the problem & finds his own solution.
In just a few minutes, she was able to increase the criteria of how the dog needs to move (adding clock positions with her reward toss). When she tosses in front of the mat, the dog has to really rethink (food is in front of him, the correct response is behind him).
There's lots for you to consider in this video. I can't stress enough how valuable I believe this skill will be to you & your training in many venues.

See you next week!

title: Tricks - Week #3 (Summer '26) - Homework
body:
Please continue to work on your foundations (nose touch, target stick, chin rest) weekly. We will build on these behaviors throughout the class.

Homework - Work on the Mat Game

Please find time to work the mat game as often as possible this week. Come to class prepared to show us your progress. 1 or 2 minutes a couple of times a day will make a huge difference in fluency. Refer to last week's email re: New Foundation Skill - Shaping a Behavior.

Please be prepared to show us how you're progressing on the mat game in next week's class. 

New Skills & Tricks

These next skills are all new foundations that will help you build many other tricks. Familiarize yourself with them & start adding them into your foundations practice to get ready to build more advanced tricks.

Roll Out the Red Carpet

Here is a variation on what we worked on in class. Note in the following video, the handler reinforced the push with a clicker & extra treats. Personally, I haven't found the need to use extra treats (golden retrievers are typically highly food motivated), but if your dog is slow-moving forward or hesitating, I would absolutely use the clicker to mark & add extra treats. 
The clicker always increases clarity in your communication, so It is never a bad idea, but since this is a self-reinforcing game, the need for it is more personal choice or dog specific.


https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o1ZqnRKZK_U

Once your dog is reliably pushing an object with its nose, you can adapt the behavior to other tricks. An easy transition is rolling a ball.

Rolling the Ball

https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=162512161755009

This technique can easily be modified for pushing other objects. Be creative & think of fun tricks to do with fun props.  (Working with your dog to be proficient at directing the ball will help you with higher level tricks. Advanced dogs: Bowling is an Advanced trick. Making a Soccer Goal is Performer level. So, practice to get the dog pushing the ball in a specific direction helps build toward tougher tricks.)

Train a Sustained Nose Touch

Learning how to get a sustained nose touch or adding duration to other behaviors is a valuable tool.

In this video, the handler isn't using a clicker, but I recommend you use the clicker to clearly communicate with your dog when the correct behavior is complete.

https://www.facebook.com/reel/1775099979793989

Once you have built a little bit of duration on a hand touch, you can train this cute, little trick.

Tell Me a Secret

https://www.facebook.com/reel/23968036912827122

Be thinking of ways you can withhold your click (or marker word) to add duration to other future tricks.

Teaching a Paw Target

The trainer thoroughly discusses how to train a paw target, and also suggests potential uses for your paw target. After you have worked on the mat game, find a new object to use as a paw target & see if you can create a new behavior using your paw target.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C4OYk7dqRus

While continuing to work on foundation skills, you are going to find that your dog will soon be adding duration, difficulty, and/or fluency. You will be able to utilize these base skills for hundreds & hundreds of behaviors so, please don't discount their value even though some are very simple.

Our goal is to help our dogs THINK all while building confidence to offer new behaviors. Once dogs are willingly offering behaviors, we can do so much to motivate them for cool tricks. Confidence is important! Your dog needs to feel safe to experiment. Also remember, REINFORCE successes (even tiny advances toward your goal), IGNORE incorrect or unwanted behavior.

Have fun & see you next week.

Jeanne

title: Tricks - (Summer '26) - Week #4 - Homework & New Tricks for All
body:
Homework


Please choose another behavior to shape & show off in class next week.  Please make sure to SHAPE the behavior (rather than lure, etc.). Use your clicker as your sole form of communication with your dog. It can be a simple or complex behavior, but I would like to see something more complex than eye contact for most dogs (especially repeating dogs), but if that is a particular problem for your dog to maintain focus, that can be your choice. Ideas for some simple behaviors are paws up on a stepstool, jump into a Chewy box, stand on a box, circle around a cone or box, mat game, etc. Please choose something you have never trained.  Remember: SHAPE IT.

 

Please also try to spend a few minutes as often as possible building fluency on foundation behaviors (nose target, target stick, chin rest, and mat game). Two minutes at a time on these behaviors every day will make a huge impact on fluency for your dog.



New Tricks to Try



Shake Hands (Novice), High Five (Novice), Wave (Intermediate)



Preferred Methods:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kwBSloRzDSk

The above method helps your dog start to think and problem solve.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=42OOTnTETNw

Note when and why this trainer uses voice markers and clicker for timing purposes.



Option: (not preferred)

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-QEuYdcP6o8

Here’s a method that I don’t particularly like but it can be effective: 1) physically manipulating the dog rather than having the dog think through the behavior, and 2) using the cue word in advance of the behavior. The dog has no idea what the word shake means so adding the cue in advance is meaningless to the dog.

 

Nose Target/Close Cabinet Door (Intermediate Trick)

Practice a few nose touches with your dog with a target similar to a dog food lid while holding it in your hand. Then, tape your nose target to a wall or door of a cabinet. The progression from hand touch to target touch should go fairly smooth as the dog will generalize the behavior if you stay close to the target. On a wall, get your dog to move away from the target with a reset cookie similar to the mat game. You gradually increase the distance for the dog. 

On a cabinet, work toward closing a cabinet door. First, make sure the dog is willingly going to the target and putting its nose on the target. Then, open the door just an inch or two so that the touch will move the door.  Work up to closing that door. Once the dog understands the game, add the cue, and you can then remove the target. At that point, move on using  the same process to close drawers. 

 

Crawl (Novice or Intermediate)

We discussed one method to teach crawl in class. This next video includes that method and two others. Any of these methods are great choices. To score the trick as Intermediate, your dog will have to stay crawling for five body lengths.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SzgAUjhGnDs&t=2s

Remember, if you are using the lure, work first with just the slightest forward movement and even the tiny muscle movement can be marked/reinforced. Don't go too far too fast or you will end up getting frustrated. That slows progress and gives you random results. Slow and steady wins this race. This trick is one of two intermediate tricks where you can always use a food lure.

 

Rollover (Intermediate)

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dCOvAf_-Xz8

NOTE: I suggest working on rollover and play dead/bang at different times. Get one of them completely fluent and on cue before working the other. These are very similar so avoid confusing your dog.



Play Dead (Advanced)

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wxrlLg_nEO4&t=8s

Take particular note of how she delivers the reward. In the beginning, she throws a reset cookie. Later, she presents food in-position to maintain the behavior. She also shows a very deliberate fading of a lure & turns it into her cue. Lots of very good skills to take note of & learn here!!! Watch it a couple of times as these skills are very precise & valuable.

 

Dramatic Bang/Play Dead (Advanced)

Here’s a good way to start getting fancy with this trick:

https://www.facebook.com/share/v/14hVZuScBbm/

 

Leg Weaves (Intermediate & Advanced)

Personally, I find it easier to teach walking leg weave before standing leg weave. AKC seems to think the difficulty is in the walking movement. I think the dog responds easier to hand target or target stick better when moving. So, here are some options for you to try. We can score the trick at both levels so it will pay off if you work both.

Homework


Please choose another behavior to shape & show off in class next week.  Please make sure to SHAPE the behavior (rather than lure, etc.). Use your clicker as your sole form of communication with your dog. It can be a simple or complex behavior, but I would like to see something more complex than eye contact for most dogs (especially repeating dogs), but if that is a particular problem for your dog to maintain focus, that can be your choice. Ideas for some simple behaviors are paws up on a stepstool, jump into a Chewy box, stand on a box, circle around a cone or box, mat game, etc. Please choose something you have never trained.  Remember: SHAPE IT.

 

Please also try to spend a few minutes as often as possible building fluency on foundation behaviors (nose target, target stick, chin rest, and mat game). Two minutes at a time on these behaviors every day will make a huge impact on fluency for your dog.

Note when and why this trainer uses voice markers and clicker for timing purposes.



Option: (not preferred)

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-QEuYdcP6o8

Here’s a method that I don’t particularly like but it can be effective: 1) physically manipulating the dog rather than having the dog think through the behavior, and 2) using the cue word in advance of the behavior. The dog has no idea what the word shake means so adding the cue in advance is meaningless to the dog.

 

Nose Target/Close Cabinet Door (Intermediate Trick)

Practice a few nose touches with your dog with a target similar to a dog food lid while holding it in your hand. Then, tape your nose target to a wall or door of a cabinet. The progression from hand touch to target touch should go fairly smooth as the dog will generalize the behavior if you stay close to the target. On a wall, get your dog to move away from the target with a reset cookie similar to the mat game. You gradually increase the distance for the dog. 

On a cabinet, work toward closing a cabinet door. First, make sure the dog is willingly going to the target and putting its nose on the target. Then, open the door just an inch or two so that the touch will move the door.  Work up to closing that door. Once the dog understands the game, add the cue, and you can then remove the target. At that point, move on using  the same process to close drawers. 

 

Crawl (Novice or Intermediate)

We discussed one method to teach crawl in class. This next video includes that method and two others. Any of these methods are great choices. To score the trick as Intermediate, your dog will have to stay crawling for five body lengths.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SzgAUjhGnDs&t=2s

Remember, if you are using the lure, work first with just the slightest forward movement and even the tiny muscle movement can be marked/reinforced. Don't go too far too fast or you will end up getting frustrated. That slows progress and gives you random results. Slow and steady wins this race. This trick is one of two intermediate tricks where you can always use a food lure.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dCOvAf_-Xz8

We will work to SHAPE mouthwork.  We want to make sure this is fun & pleasant for the dogs. Please collect a few items to bring to class with different textures (wood, plastic, cloth, metal, etc.) for shaping the take/hold if you can gather some. Try to find items your dog won't find objectionable or uncomfortably sized. Please NEVER force a dog to put an object in its mouth. You will create aversion to it. Wait until class if you are at all unsure about how to proceed.

Always take your time with mouthwork training sessions. Please don’t push too hard, fast, or use anything resembling force holds. Use short sessions & stop on a positive note. Just a few attempts & then work on something different or take a break. 

This can be frustrating for the dog & handler if you find objects that the dog doesn’t like to hold or you get stuck and allow frustration. Try to avoid those things & find something fun like a toy that the dog is happy to hold if you’re running into resistance. Making little bits of progress with a happy, motivated dog will go a lot farther than pushing a reluctant dog into doing a trick that it hates.

title: Tricks - Week #5 (Summer '26) - Shaping vs. Luring
body:
This fantastic post was shared on Facebook on the Agility Campus page. Lenore Dubaldo shared this post with me. She helped me create TDTC's original Tricks program back in 2017. I'm excited to share it with you. The author is discussing how this applies to agility; however, I believe it applies to most/all types of training.

The post discusses what I have described as our attempt to create a thinking dog who offers behaviors & retains skills better. The author shares a little bit of the science & is far more eloquent explaining the concept.

https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1BckGpjn1m/ When you lure your dog through a behavior, here's what lights up:

- Motor cortex (following movement)
- Visual cortex (tracking the food)
- Reward pathway (getting the food)
- Prefrontal cortex → barely active

When you shape the same behavior:

- Motor cortex (trying movements)
- Prefrontal cortex → HIGHLY active (problem-solving, decision-making)
- Hippocampus engaged (pattern recognition, memory formation)
- Reward pathway (getting food AND solving the problem)
- Different areas of the brain. Different learning.

Here's why it matters for agility:

The prefrontal cortex is where executive function lives. Planning. Decision-making. Flexible thinking. Inhibitory control. Working memory.

These aren't bonus skills. These are EXACTLY what your dog needs to:

- Plan a line
- Decide which obstacle to take
- Adjust to your handling
- Control impulses at the start line
- Remember cues

You can't build executive function through luring. The brain regions you'd need to train aren't even engaged.

But there's a second cost most handlers don't see:

Motor learning without cognitive engagement needs far more repetition.

When the prefrontal cortex isn't active, the dog isn't building understanding — he's building muscle memory. And muscle memory alone takes WAY more reps to stick.


You can drill weave entries 200 times and still watch the behavior fall apart under pressure.

A shaped dog might learn the same skill in a fraction of the reps. Because his brain encoded it as a concept, not just a movement.

Same skill. Half the work. More resilient under stress.

Shape once. Drill less.


👉Have you ever drilled and drilled a behavior that still falls apart under pressure?



Enjoy! See you in class!

Jeanne

title: Luka and the Mat Game
body:
Luka & the Mat Game

https://youtu.be/SEWi09wyspw

The mat game is a great tool to have in your tool box. I decided to play the mat game with my dog, Luka, who is four, and show how the mat game can move forward from a bath mat, to smaller things, and even a tape target stuck to the floor.

The video is unedited, and our session runs a bit long, but overall, I'm happy with the session. I think that it really shows how the mat game is beneficial for teaching targeting, but also things like go outs, and behaviors where sending the dog to a specific location is needed.


Session Walk Through

When we start, I go get my mat, which is a pretty large rug. I fold it in half to get the game started. As you can see, Luka immediately goes to the mat and gets his click, then the reset cookie.

After a couple reps, I make the mat a bit smaller, but the game stays the same. Luka has been playing the mat game since I brought him home as a puppy. It may take your dog longer to realize the mat game is the same, even if the size and shape of the mat changes.

Around 1:15 I run out of cookies and have to pause to get more. Notice I do this after the reset cookie is thrown, and I have no expectation of Luka continuing to play the game, but he does go to the mat before coming back to me. I then send him back to the mat and begin again.

Around 1:45 I add a yellow circle target to the mat. The game doesn't change, but my criteria does. I want him to step on the circle target. After a couple reps, I remove the large mat completely, and leave only the yellow circle. 

Around 2:30 I swap the yellow target for a purple target with an "X" made from masking tape. We're still in the same general area we started in, but we've changed "mats" a number of times. Overall, the game still has not changed.

Notice when he steps over the target, and not on it, I withhold the click, and he self corrects. He doesn't offer another behavior, he moves his feet to touch the target. You can see this around 2:45 for a couple of reps.

Usually we'd end around the three minute mark, and while he's getting slower, he's still actively engaging with the game, so I continue. I've now removed the circle target completely, and put the "X" down in the same general area. Luka continues the game.

Around 3:35-40, I move the tape target completely to the corner of our work area. Luka now opts out completely, going to his cot, then coming back. He circles back around to me and just looks at me. I move my body to try and keep him working, but his sniffing behavior also shows he's really no longer interested. I continue shuffling my feet around until he eventually goes to the target.

The one good thing about the video being so long is that you can see how I get him to re-engage, while staying quiet. I use my body language to try and get him to interact with the target again. We're completely done when he pulls the target off the floor. Again, I know I went too long, but he did re-engage, just not with the same enthusiasm.

Things that could be improved:

1. I didn't plan things out before I started recording, so I'm having to dig out my mat and the markers I want to use for the game. While Luka doesn't mind, being better prepared would help keep our session focused and moving forward instead of pausing to swap out props.

2. I did not have enough cookies in my pocket when I started. Like improvement one, Luka doesn't mind, but the fewer breaks we have in the middle, the better he does overall. 

3. Luka clearly opts out by going to his cot, but I pulled him back into the game. Usually I would take this opt out for what it is, and end the game there. For the purposes of this video, I wanted to show how moving the target to a different location shouldn't prevent the dog from successfully finding the target. This is because the mat (or target) is well generalized.

Other things of note:

My body language is pretty subdued. Luka is a high drive dog and tends to get over aroused pretty easily. When we're training, I try to keep his energy low so that he stays focused. If your dog is less keen, you may need to be more exciting than I am. A good way to do this is starting the game with fast paced "cookie tossing" where you throw a cookie, the dog gets it, re-orients to you, then gets another cookie.

Since Luka is familiar with the game, we can easily move through multiple mats in one session, but we could start with a small target and just use the small target, or even the tape target. You don't have to change mat sizes like we did, I just wanted to show the versatility once your dog is fluent with the game.

Remember to keep practicing and have fun! See you next week!

Melanie
